query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of HCP elements does not improve room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, or if it compromises high-temperature mechanical performance and BCC structural stability, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: W-based refractory HEAs (RHEAs) have been recently developed in the context of high-temperature applications, showing high melting temperature (above 2873 K) and superior mechanical strength at high temperatures compared to Ni-based superalloys or pure W,. Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. decision.trend: The trend in the research on refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) is to improve their room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while maintaining their high-temperature mechanical performance and BCC structural stability. Various approaches have been explored, including microstructural engineering, alloy design, and processing routes. The studies have shown that the addition of HCP elements to BCC RHEAs can enhance ductility, and that the ratio of HCP to BCC elements can control the ductility and strength of RHEAs.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved problem is to achieve a balance between room-temperature ductility, irradiation tolerance, and high-temperature mechanical performance in RHEAs. The current RHEAs often suffer from poor room-temperature ductility and unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks under irradiation.
decision.lever: addition of HCP elements to BCC RHEAs
decision.why: The addition of HCP elements to BCC RHEAs has been shown to enhance ductility and can potentially improve irradiation tolerance. This approach is a relatively simple way to optimize the mechanical properties of RHEAs and can be explored further to achieve a balance between room-temperature ductility, irradiation tolerance, and high-temperature mechanical performance.
